💡 Key Takeaways
  • The housing market remains tough this winter—but prepared buyers will be presented with opportunities.
  • "Preparation is everything," notes Erik Schmitt, head of consumer direct sales at Chase Home Lending, which is part of JPMorgan Chase's commercial bank.
  • The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report demonstrates that prices on upcoming homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The housing market remains tough this winter—but prepared buyers will be presented with opportunities.

"Preparation is everything," notes Erik Schmitt, head of consumer direct sales at Chase Home Lending, which is part of JPMorgan Chase's commercial bank.

The outlook for 2027 appears tough. The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report demonstrates that prices on upcoming homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers. Many have stated they expect difficulty for much of next year.

It has been revealed that on top of that, leaders at the Federal Reserve have signaled that they're poised to raise interest rates multiple times in the next few months to tame inflation. Homeowners are also managing rising insurance costs, HOA fees, and utilities.

Do anything you can now to improve your credit, pay down debt, and understand your budget and what you can afford will help, says Schmitt.

"Get pre-approval because you never know when the market will turn," he advises.

Improving credit scores and paying off higher interest-rate debt will give you more purchasing power.

This week, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low. Meanwhile, the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index revealed home values fell for the 16th straight month.

According to recent reports, so, in the coming winter there's no question about seasonal weakness in the housing market. In some markets, that means more negotiating power and possibly some better options for buyers. But shrinking inventory might also mean there are fewer options.

For that reason, Schmitt states it's best to be proactive this winter.

According to recent reports, "It's difficult to time the rate environment," says Schmitt. "What we advise customers to do is have a strong understanding of what they can afford and what they feel comfortable with. It's difficult to time the market, so if you get in a home that meets your needs, meets your affordability target, in the event rates do rally or reduce, you can always refinance.".

From Nov. 30  to Dec. 13, Chase is running a mortgage rate sale of up to 0.25% off for qualified buyers. Both new and existing customers will be able to lock in a lower rate on a new home purchase or refinance loan.

The rate sale discount can be stacked with all existing available Chase Home Lending discounts and programs like its Chase Homebuyer Grant and Relationship Pricing Program.

The stacked savings are still subject to the same terms and conditions, and other programs must have structure that means maximum discounts and limitations.

The bank determined a lot of good buyers remain on the sidelines.

Industry observers note that JPMorgan Chase confirmed earlier this year it would invest $750 billion into the housing market. Its American Dream Initiative aims to build or preserve 1 million affordable housing units and help a half-million customers purchase homes—including 200,000 first-time homebuyers.

"Our focus is where we can help with affordability," says Schmitt.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Epochal debuts with $100M to help developers train predictive AI models

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc.
  • The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp.
  • Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. launched today with $100 million in funding.

The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The manufacturer’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.

After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the tech giant, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.

Recent findings suggest that according to Epochal, its service mitigates the concern by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a tech giant is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

Recent findings suggest that the Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal plans to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

From Honky-Tonks to High-End Estates: Inside Nashville’s Lasting Luxury Boom

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many metros gave up most or even all of their COVID-19 pandemic-era housing market gains, but some kept on trucking, including Nashville, TN.
  • "Nashville is one of the pandemic boomtowns that kept its boom," writes Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith in his Nashville Luxury Market Highlight report.
  • Nashville held on to more of its pandemic run-up than any other major Tennessee metro as of September 2026, says the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many metros gave up most or even all of their COVID-19 pandemic-era housing market gains, but some kept on trucking, including Nashville, TN.

"Nashville is one of the pandemic boomtowns that kept its boom," writes Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith in his Nashville Luxury Market Highlight report.

Nashville held on to more of its pandemic run-up than any other major Tennessee metro as of September 2026, says the report.

Industry observers note that while the area has been hot for years, demand for its luxury homes accelerated sharply after the pandemic, resulting in a 100% increase in prices from February 2020 to October 2026. Unlike other metros that gave up most or even all of its pandemic-era gains, Nashville has retained a healthy 83.3% of them.

During the pandemic, remote work allowed many people to relocate to Music City, where they could enjoy not only the conveniences and excitement of city life, but also lower prices than wherever they were coming from.

Sources indicate that and unlike other midsized metros that saw massive pandemic-era gains—such as Denver and Austin, TX—Nashville's prices have kept afloat. Denver, on the other hand, sits 33% below its pandemic peak, and Austin is 29% below.

According to recent reports, nashville's entry-luxury threshold (the top 10% of listings) now stands at $1.65 million versus $899,000 at the start of the pandemic in February 2020. This is only 8.4% below its peak of $1.80 million in April 2022.

In a recent development, in terms of retention, the only Tennessee city that comes out slightly ahead of Nashville is Knoxville, which pulled ahead in October with a 86.4% retention rate from its pandemic-era highs. But Nashville had to hold on to steeper gains, because its run-up was twice as large as Knoxville's.

Knoxville's entry-luxury threshold currently stands at $1.05 million, a smidge below its peak median price of $1.10 million in May 2023.

Another standout in the state is Chattanooga, which has retained nearly 64% of its pandemic gains, while Cleveland, TN, which had the highest run-up of any metro in the state with 137%, has given up all but 28.6% of that.

Nashville's share of luxury listings has also continued to rise, with million-dollar-plus homes making up 18.9% of its listings in September 2026, up from a mere 8.3% five years ago.

This is 4.6 times more luxe listings than in 2020 and is the highest percentage in the state.

Drilling down deeper, the priciest area in the metro is the newly introduced-construction haven of Williamson County. Within the county, College Grove (ZIP code 37046) has the steepest price tags, with a median list price of $3,193,165 and a luxury threshold of $7,209,900.

A full 91% of College Grove's home listings are over one million dollars, behind only Arrington at 96%.

Here, grand estates, often upcoming, boast a median 5,304 square feet of space, significantly larger than the second-place finisher, Nashville (Oak Hill) at 4,015 square feet. It also has the highest per-square-foot price at $578.

In a recent development, "We've always remained in a bubble," states local real estate broker Susan Gregory. "Even when the market turned in 2008, we weren't devastated like the rest of the country. Our newly introduced construction kept selling, and we kept building.".

She attributes the area's pricing resilience to an excellent public school system, as well as generous estates and sizable plots that lure top earners in numerous industries. Of course, Music City is known for its country crooning residents such as Keith Urban, Faith Hill and Tim McGraw, Jason Aldean, or the late Dolly Parton.

"There's a lot of country music stars and rock bands that retire out here," claims Gregory. Elite music industry types like to snap up anywhere from 60 to 100 acres of farmland. This enables them to have lots of privacy and ranchlike living while not giving up the amenities of downtown Nashville, only a half-hour's drive away.

And don't forget those who are still migrating to the Southern state from higher-taxed pastures.

According to recent reports, "I just sold a house to a couple from Connecticut, and they are like, 'We just got a huge raise, just in taxes,'" the agent tells Realtor.com. She claims that with their move, the couple's property taxes dropped from around $30,000 a year to approximately $8,000.

Such wealthy incomers were mostly responsible for the area's run-up, says the broker.

"They were offering stupid money," she says of pandemic-era buyers who would "overbid" on properties. "Our prices doubled, tripled, and quadrupled.".

Around this time, she adds, Williamson County changed its zoning so that subdivision lots had to be at least 5 acres—a common tactic employed to rein in development and protect an area's "character.".

"Being on 5 acres increases values significantly," she states.

In Nashville proper, the Oak Hill neighborhood's luxury threshold of $5,815,000 is the second highest in the metro.

While the city remains famous for its music mavens, it is also increasingly a hub for nonmusic industries like healthcare, tech, and even finance.

Business behemoths such as Nissan, In-N-Out Burger, Oracle, and AllianceBernstein have been drawn to the city thanks to low or even no taxes.

High corporate earners are swarming newly introduced luxury buildings such as the Four Seasons Private Residences and the Residences at Broadwest, which sits atop the Conrad Nashville, part of the Hilton franchise. At the Four Seasons, which is sold out, price tags range from a hefty $5.16 million to $33.5 million.

In trendy, retail-friendly neighborhood The Gulch, The Residences at The Nashville Edition is being built atop the 261-room Edition hotel.

In the sleek, full-service tower, one-bedroom condos start at $1.62 million and four-bedrooms at $8.65 million.

For Corcoran Reverie agent Kris Wylder, prices like these are on par with Nashville's newish luxury market and scene.

It has been revealed that "When I first came here, I thought, 'This city is so undervalued for what it is and what it has to offer,'" she previously told Realtor.com. "It has exploded from an amenity standpoint: the restaurants, the health and wellness options, the shopping. It's just been incredible to see.

In a recent development, "To me, [Nashville] is finally just being valued where it should be. I'm like, 'Oh finally, the prices caught up with everything this city has to offer.'".

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. Her work can be found in news outlets worldwide, including Yahoo, SF Gate, New York Post, Seattle-Post Intelligencer, Marie Claire, She Knows, Huffington Post, and New York Magazine. She has an M.A. in journalism from Columbia University. In her spare time, she writes psychological thrillers under a pen name. She lives in Brooklyn, and her cat foster Instagram account has over 4 million views.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Employees working at frontier artificial intelligence model companies Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC have been butting heads with executives over advanced models whose reasoning is such that the models pose to danger to humanity, according to a report by Axios today based on more than two dozen sources familiar with the current standoff at the companies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:41 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Employees working at frontier artificial intelligence model companies Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC have been butting heads with executives over advanced models whose reasoning is such that the models pose to danger to humanity, according to a report by Axios today based on more than two dozen sources familiar with the current standoff at the companies.

The report states the models in question are far more powerful than anything that has so far reached the public, showing great leaps forward in reasoning in many areas that have been difficult, “if not impossible,” to control during tests. It appears that some staff err on the side of caution and believe the training should stop completely while others believe they can be reined in.

In a recent development, “If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us… they will in fact be able to trick us successfully,” one of the researchers told Axios. “And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.”.

Industry observers note that after Open AI’s AI agents seemingly went berserk earlier this year and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc., there have been calls to pause AI development until safety can be assured. The state of California this month introduced a lawsuit calling Open AI a “public nuisance,” whose models right now pose cybersecurity risks while threatening the “well-being of society.”.

Recent findings suggest that the debate on how far we should go before we step on the brakes has largely been overshadowed by companies, and the countries where they are developed, steaming ahead winning the AI race. In the Axios report, many of the anonymous claimed executives are “out of touch” with safety issues as they put profit first.

Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei has been vocal about the “existential risks to humanity” that AI might bring. In his recent essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei said “pacing” is important, warning that authoritarian regimes such as China must agree to cooperate in moving forward slowly with the frontier models. President Trump has been less than supportive of such measures, calling the threats to humanity a “hoax.”.

Rajiv Ramaswami to step down as Nutanix begins hunt for its next CEO

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.
  • In a recent development, in a letter to firm employees, Ramaswami (pictured) remarked he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition.
  • Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

In a recent development, in a letter to firm employees, Ramaswami (pictured) remarked he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

Industry observers note that “Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this firm and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

Sources indicate that ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the organization delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

Industry observers note that the company reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

According to recent reports, nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the company guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Recent findings suggest that investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Industry observers note that virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the tech giant during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami remarked he believes the firm is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

Sources indicate that “[We have] transformed the company to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami stated. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

According to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the new era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

According to recent reports, ramaswami’s departure from the organization should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix unveiled it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the firm by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

In April, Ramaswami appeared on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s mobile livestreaming studio, where he talked about how Nutanix is shifting away from HCI to focus on more of a “disaggregated infrastructure” strategy to support demand for autonomous AI agents:.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

I Found a Real Estate ‘Unicorn’: 2 Homes, 1 Mortgage, and $187K a Year

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thinking about investing in real estate, but not sure what to buy?
  • When Steve Kwong ran the numbers on his first traditional investment property, he realized a single broken water heater would wipe out an entire year of profits.
  • So, the 48-year-old Orlando Realtor® walked away from the deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thinking about investing in real estate, but not sure what to buy? Welcome to "My First Deal," where real people spill about how they chose what to invest in, how they found the property, and how that deal is performing. If you have a story to share about your investor journey, email news@realtor.com.

When Steve Kwong ran the numbers on his first traditional investment property, he realized a single broken water heater would wipe out an entire year of profits.

So, the 48-year-old Orlando Realtor® walked away from the deal. Then, he teamed up with a business partner, Rob Leventhal—owner of STR pricing, a revenue management service—and pivoted to short-term rentals.

According to recent reports, they searched for three months before buying what Kwong calls a real estate "unicorn": two homes on one lot in Pigeon Forge, TN, with one mortgage. Combined, the two homes grossed $187,000 in 2021—a banner year for most short-term rentals.

Max budget: $475,000Asking price: $479,000Closing price: $462,000Down payment: $92,400Mortgage: $2,390Taxes: $3,040.

Originally, I was going to buy a long-term rental on a golf course in Apopka, FL, and would be renting to a friend. I got under contract, but decided not to close. I ran the numbers and would have made $300 a month, which is one capital expense away from not making any money in a year.

It has been revealed that I was talking to my friend Rob, who had friends who wanted to buy STRs. This was 2019. We decided to form a partnership and buy something together. We did our research and found Realtor Avery Carl of The Short Term Shop. Everything online led us to buy in the Smoky Mountains—specifically Pigeon Forge, TN.

We relied on Avery to guide us. She advised us that we didn’t want a one- or two-bedroom property. We were looking to spend around $450,000. We were also relying on the data, which told us which parts of town would be good.

It has been revealed that avery and her team did video tours of other homes we were interested in. This was the only one we saw in person.

It was already performing really well. When we were interested in anything, we asked Avery to get the financials to see what the average nightly rate was and what they spent on cleaning. We liked the location. This is down the road from The Island, which is one of the biggest attractions in Pigeon Forge. It also had a private, wooded lot. What drew us to this one most of all was that we were getting two properties on the same lot for one mortgage—it’s a unicorn.

We figured we could bring in higher numbers than what the previous owners had done because we did a lot of research. We had taken a seminar with Richard Fertig and watched all of his videos about how to provide an exceptional guest experience. The industry was at a turning point back then, with people just starting to realize they could do this remotely. We were confident if we implemented all those strategies we would hit a home run.

We offered around $450,000 and settled on $462,000.

It has been revealed that we put 20% down. We could have put down less, but we were told that if we ever had to exit in a bad market, we would be at an advantage to sell if we put more down.

From my real estate commissions, and my business partner saved income from his W-2 job (at the time, he worked for a law firm).

Sources indicate that as soon as we listed, we got bookings. In the first three months, we made enough to pay the first year of mortgage payments. The first year, we grossed $87,000 and we thought that was good. Our best year was 2021 when we grossed $187,000. The all-in cost to run these for the year is about $45,000 to $50,000, which includes mortgage and expenses. In 2021, that meant bringing in $137,000. That mentioned, we self-manage, so we are not paying 20% to a vacation property manager.

In a recent development, the $187,000 was a [COVID-19] pandemic year, and Tennessee was one of the first states to open. We knew that number wouldn’t be realistic over time. The average gross per year is closer now to $120,000.

Recent findings suggest that you have to continually educate yourself with what is going on in the industry. You will be left behind if you're not up on the newest trends and technology. There is also so much competition.

Recent findings suggest that we hired a VA to help answer messages. At night, we use a little bit of AI.

In a recent development, these two Airbnbs, the four-bedroom and the one-bedroom, helped us save up to buy other properties. We now have four more, including a pool cabin in Gatlinburg, TN, a property in Blue Ridge, GA, and one in Broken Bow, OK.

It has been revealed that there are a lot of things I love. Part of it is sentimental because this was our first one. Also, if you’re going to invest in a property, it’s nice to have an asset that you can use and enjoy. You don’t get that with a long-term rental. I never bought any STRs locally because I wanted vacations. I take my brother and his family every year to this property, and that’s the most fun part.

Tech Report: Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different.
  • It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.
  • Sources indicate that the organization mentioned today that people can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

Sources indicate that the organization mentioned today that people can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

Industry observers note that however, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant users first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic noted people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the manufacturer said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s newly introduced “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

In a video posted on X, Anthropic indicated how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq.

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026.

Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic stated.

Sources indicate that as an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic noted. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

Sources indicate that there is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”.

It has been revealed that that could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

#169294. How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (869 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.
  • The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing.
  • In a recent development, the study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.

The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing. This comes as state lawmakers have proposed many latest laws this year to curtail policies that stall building, with mixed success.

In a recent development, the study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws. Both of these kinds of disputes are expensive and time-consuming. Developers have to examine and reexamine the environmental impact of developments they want to build, and courts must then determine what cities are required to do to ensure a clean environment for residents.

"A real cost is borne on the people who are renting and buying those homes and apartments," Kyle Sweetland, the study's author, tells Realtor.com®.

About a dozen states have pitched laws that would make it easier to build homes, many of them by reducing zoning or lot size requirements. But some proposals have also met with failure, like California's Proposition 45, which aimed to expedite project reviews through the California Environmental Quality Act.

The Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap research shows the U.S. faces a shortage of 4.03 million homes. Our Let America Build campaign has tracked how states have responded to this shortage, and which are tackling the problem.

Recent findings suggest that california has a long history of slow development on account of environmental review. In one recent example, a 49-unit housing development was stalled for 4.5 years in environmental litigation, which the developer said had raised the cost of the project by $9 million. In another, a 34-home subdivision was stalled for nearly 40 years, in part because of neighbors' environmental concerns.

It's not just a California problem. Sweetland looked at 16 states and the District of Columbia that have environmental policy acts that affect developers, or amendments that affect municipalities. Wyoming, Minnesota, Newly introduced York, Hawaii, and Massachusetts have both.

But other protections are also in place in California, Nevada, Washington, North Dakota, Illinois, Wyoming, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Upcoming Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia.

According to recent reports, it's hard to track precisely how much this kind of litigation drives up the costs of housing. Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner also notes that it's hard to tell how many housing projects didn't start in the first place because developers expected a lawsuit.

"The bigger costs come from what the lawsuit does to the project’s financing and schedule," Berner says. "Appeals typically add years, and in the meantime, most projects can’t secure construction or grant funding. Loans, taxes, and insurance keep accruing, and construction costs can rise while the project waits.".

Change could come at the federal level. Last week, the Senate passed a controversial bill that would reduce some federal environmental regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, to speed up construction of significant-energy projects. Environmental groups opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which next heads to the House.

In some instances, the environmental lawsuits don't actually produce better outcomes for the environment. Seattle found that just 16% of cases filed using environmental laws over the 2010s resulted in decisions requiring environmental remediation. In New York, about 22% of cases over 15 years resulted in more environmental reviews, an outside researcher found.

According to recent reports, berner says the balance is that environmental laws are sometimes the easiest avenue residents have to oppose a residential project. It's just a matter of not abusing the process.

"While challenging a project is a relatively cheap thing to do, being on the receiving end of a legal battle can derail a project even without going all the way through the litigation process," Berner claims. "This uncertainty adds to the cost of capital for builders and squeezes out lower-margin projects like affordable and infill housing.".

Pacific Legal Foundation says one solution for these concerns is to narrow the scope of some environmental laws. For instance, Sweetland says legal challenges from outside environmental groups could be limited. That way, the people challenging housing developments have a real vested interest in their outcomes.

He also suggests requirements that groups that lose cases have to pay the legal fees. That isn't typical everywhere, even if developers pay the legal fees when they lose. That provides some incentive that those launching lawsuits have a legitimate claim, as opposed to using the courts as a stalling tactic.

"The law shouldn't just give anybody the ability to have a license to stop a building from moving forward," Sweetland claims.

Recent findings suggest that tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

In a recent development, positive developments around a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill clearing a House committee also offered a modest sentiment boost, reminding investors that longer-term institutional and policy interest has not disappeared.

Even as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs continued to post outflows (including a sizable figure on the prior session), the market rose anyway. This divergence often signals that stronger hands are absorbing remaining sellers or that short covering is outweighing institutional redemptions in the short term.

It has been revealed that bitcoin’s ability to reclaim and hold above $60,000 after testing lower support is particularly constructive. A series of higher lows on the daily chart, if sustained, would mark a potential shift in short-term market structure.

If ETF outflows begin to slow or reverse in the coming sessions, and if upcoming economic data softens rate-hike expectations, the path higher would open more clearly.

Institutional accumulation has continued in the background even during the recent drawdown, and any improvement in broader risk sentiment could amplify the move. For now, today’s rebound offers the first tangible evidence in days that the worst of the immediate selling may be behind the market.

Whether it becomes a durable rally will depend on follow-through volume and Bitcoin’s ability to defend the $60,000 area, but the green candles offer a welcome dose of hope to those eagerly wondering why crypto is up today.

#169291. Latest Update: Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1404 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, zoom Communications Inc.
  • Recent findings suggest that total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters.
  • The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the manufacturer outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 23:43 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

According to recent reports, zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video tech giant everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, revealed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Recent findings suggest that total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and revealed its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the manufacturer outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

It has been revealed that the concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

It has been revealed that nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”.

Industry observers note that AI agents are promptly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually remarked to one another and to customers.

In a recent development, “Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan stated. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

According to recent reports, my Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan noted it is nearing 2 million monthly active customers, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

Recent findings suggest that A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers newly introduced to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh upcoming way.” Specifically, she noted, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a massive winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

Recent findings suggest that there is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan noted. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another manufacturer’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a manufacturer that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”.

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the organization is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

Sources indicate that that is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.
  • Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into fresh markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies.
  • Industry observers note that eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into fresh markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it looks to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

Industry observers note that eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

According to recent reports, engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the organization. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, claims it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa noted in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Recent findings suggest that jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen remarked in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl stated in a statement.

Sources indicate that howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter remarked in a statement.

Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that just three of the 50 most populous U.S.
  • Industry observers note that nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers.
  • Industry observers note that all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Industry observers note that nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

Industry observers note that all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

According to recent reports, the seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater Fresh York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” mentioned Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially key to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”.

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

According to recent reports, when sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

In a recent development, we estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

In a recent development, it’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

Recent findings suggest that “A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate. With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”.

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

In a recent development, there were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

According to recent reports, on the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

In a recent development, the number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more upcoming listings are adding to the substantial pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a upcoming job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

It has been revealed that over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

Industry observers note that the Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add fresh homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

Industry observers note that the surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

It has been revealed that as a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Fresh Haven Weighs Sweeping Ban on Non-Owner-Occupied Airbnb Rentals—Will It Actually Lower Rents?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homeowners and short-term rental hosts in New Haven, CT, are watching closely as city lawmakers weigh a sweeping proposal that would largely prohibit short-term rentals in the city.
  • Alderpersons Leland Moore, Frank Douglas, and Mandy Martinelli proposed OR-2026-0039 this past October.
  • Residents who live in their home could still host short-term stays in their primary residences as long as they obtained a city home-sharing license, remained in the home during the rental, and followed occupancy limits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homeowners and short-term rental hosts in New Haven, CT, are watching closely as city lawmakers weigh a sweeping proposal that would largely prohibit short-term rentals in the city.

Alderpersons Leland Moore, Frank Douglas, and Mandy Martinelli proposed OR-2026-0039 this past October. The ordinance would bar rentals of 30 days or less in properties that are not a host’s primary residence starting on March 31, 2027. Hosts operating full-time vacation rentals or investor units would need to switch to long-term leases of more than 30 days.

Residents who live in their home could still host short-term stays in their primary residences as long as they obtained a city home-sharing license, remained in the home during the rental, and followed occupancy limits.

"The conversion of long-term residential housing into short-term rentals inflates rental prices, reduces housing inventory, and directly contributes to the displacement of long-term neighbors and residents from communities," the ordinance reads in part.

Sources indicate that supporters of the measure argue it will help free up units in the housing-strapped city. Opponents say it will do little to improve affordability and will hurt residents who make a living from renting out their properties.

It has been revealed that at a Nov. 16 Board of Alders meeting where the board was to take a final vote on the measure, more than a hundred residents packed City Hall. Alderman Richard Furlow ultimately tabled the vote until Dec. 7, giving members more time to review proposed amendments to the initiative.

The measure has been supported by housing affordability advocates, hotel and hospitality labor unions, and the city's mayor, Justin Elicker.

Recent findings suggest that "We want to make sure homeowners, if they have an extra room or extra apartment in their building, have the ability to rent," Elicker told NBC affiliate WVIT. "But at the same time, we're in an affordability crisis right now, and housing affordability is something that's affecting so many Upcoming Haven residents. We have a lot of new construction in the city. A lot of that’s affordable, but a lot of that’s not.".

The advocacy group New Haven Rising has argued that short-term rentals drive up housing costs for residents and cannibalize local rental stock, keeping locals locked out of homes.

A separate group, Put New Haven First, came out against the proposed ban, noting that the city had yet to complete an economic impact study of the ordinance.

For its part, Airbnb has argued that the proposed ban will hurt locals who make a living by renting out their properties and "puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”.

It has been revealed that “Airbnb listings make up just 0.5% of the city’s total housing stock," a company spokesperson tells Realtor.com®. "Restricting them won’t lower rents or improve housing availability, but it will take away income that helps local homeowners stay in their homes and supports the house cleaners, landscapers, and small businesses who serve guests.

Industry observers note that "Short-term rentals also give visiting families, including those in town for the hospital or university, flexible and affordable places to stay that hotels often can't match," the statement continued. "Residents have asked the Board of Alders to study the impact before acting, and we urge them to look at the evidence before passing a bill that puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”.

Newly introduced Haven is home to Yale University, a world-class hospital system, more than 70 biotech companies, and a burgeoning pizza tourism industry. Locals love its walkability, proximity to nature, and food scene—but they don’t love the city’s struggling housing market.

It has been revealed that between 2020 and 2025, Fresh Haven added 3,535 housing units—more than any other Connecticut city. Yet, the city is still considered one of the worst places in the country for renters. It ranked 138 out of 182 cities on WalletHub's 2026 list of the best places to rent. The city’s median rent is $2,000 a month—more expensive than median rents in 42 of the top 50 metros.

The Realtor.com 2026 Housing Mismatch Report found that New Haven lacks homes for middle-class homebuyers.

Industry observers note that "The data makes clear that more inventory alone won’t be enough to unlock the housing market," Danielle Hale, chief economist of Realtor.com, previously mentioned. "A true recovery requires homes at the right price points.”.

There are currently 559 rental units available in the city, a 38% increase year over year. By comparison, Newly introduced Haven has approximately 765 active short-term rental listings across Airbnb, Vrbo, and Booking.com—a 19.1% decrease in active supply compared to October 2025, according to short-term rental tracking site AirDNA.

Proponents of the short-term rental ban have argued that the short-term rentals have had a deleterious effect on the city’s affordability by taking up housing stock that might otherwise be available to locals.

Industry observers note that but those 765 units make up just 2% of the city’s 38,621 rental units, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

What’s more, in other communities where short-term rentals have been curbed or prohibited, the impact on rental prices has been debatable.

In a recent development, in September 2023, Fresh York City implemented Local Law 18, which requires short-term rental hosts to live in the unit and be present during stays. That slashed short-term rental listings by more than 90%, from roughly 38,500 down to around 3,000 to 3,500 registered hosts, according to city reports and a 2026 study.

That study found that the crackdown on short-term rentals had no demonstrable impact on rents and that median monthly rents in Manhattan climbed to a record $4,700 during that period.

According to recent reports, A 2024 study from researchers at the College of William & Mary, Purdue University, and Chinese University of Hong Kong examined a similar short-term rental ban in Irvine, CA. According to their research, the ban led to a 23.1% decrease in Airbnb listings and a 2.7% decrease in rental prices. However, the period of study happened to coincide with the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Residents are eager to hear what amendments to the proposed short-term rental ban the alders will propose at the Dec. 7 meeting.

Sun Queen, a co-founder of Black Lives Matter Upcoming Haven and an organizer with the Unhoused Activists Community Team, told the New Haven Independent that short-term rentals can be useful transitional housing for unhoused people.

"I think more time was needed to do more research," she said. "I get it from all angles. We are in a housing crisis.”.

Realtor.com reached out to Martinelli, Moore, and Douglas for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, formal verification startup Sequent Inc.
  • Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set.
  • Curve also figures in how Sequent got started.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

According to recent reports, formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today unveiled that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Recent findings suggest that following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who stated AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Recent findings suggest that along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

Industry observers note that according to the post, Schwartz's portfolio reportedly went from 26 million XRP, 1,500 BTC and 40,000 ETH to just 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH. The author called it "an insane reduction" and also referred to Schwartz as the current CTO of Ripple, while he now holds the emeritus title.

Sources indicate that schwartz replied that the timeline in the post was wrong. "That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade," he wrote. As proof, he shared his own post from April 21, 2019. In that post, Schwartz said he was still sticking to the "de-risking strategy" that he and his wife agreed on when they first decided to put their own money into crypto. He also admitted back then that selling during the bull run "still hurt.".

In a recent development, at the same time, Schwartz did not dispute the numbers themselves. "But it's basically true. I hate risk. I can't help it," he wrote in a follow-up post. According to him, pretty much every massive risk he has ever taken has worked out well, and rationally he should be taking more risk as he gets wealthier. "But I hate it. I just hate risk and can't do anything about it," Schwartz added.

In a recent development, that wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade. You can find me talking about this in many posts over the years, like this one:https://t.co/5MgcPZ5qyG.

At press time, XRP was trading at around $0.939, Bitcoin at $61,477 and Ethereum at $1,722. At these prices, the remaining 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH are worth about $2.89 million, and XRP accounts for more than 97% of this sum.

For comparison, at current prices, the peak holdings mentioned in the post would be worth over $185 million, with Bitcoin alone accounting for about half of it.

According to recent reports, schwartz has already explained his sales several times this year. In May, he said he did not have much XRP left and had tried to move most of his assets, other than Ripple stock, away from crypto exposure. In July, he said he regrets selling XRP at $0.10 and ETH at around $1, but noted that he and his wife had agreed to sell at every new all-time high.

Earlier in November, Schwartz disclosed that he sold about 2.5 million XRP in 2025. Per Schwartz, most of these tokens were received in 2020 and 2023, and he paid approximately $1.7 million in capital gains tax on those sales. He shared this in response to a user who called XRP a "terrible investment.".

Sources indicate that among other things, Schwartz has previously said that his main exposure to the crypto sector now comes through Ripple stock, not XRP. In March, Ripple launched a share buyback of up to $750 million that valued the manufacturer at $50 billion.

Cardano saw a death cross in November 2025, and the same is happening this November.

The signal in November 2025 was followed by months of falling prices, which has led some to speculate that the cryptocurrency may have further downside or a recovery ahead of the end of 2026. The current uncertainty in the market has added to concerns. A volatile weekend saw Cardano fall as low as $0.134, its weakest level since December 2020, before rebounding. Sources indicate that whether that rebound holds is the test traders will keep an eye on. The $0.18 area represents an initial resistance level, while a stronger recovery toward the $0.198 to $0.20 range would bring Cardano closer to its daily moving averages.

Sources indicate that another possibility is sideways trading as ADA attempts to establish a sustainable bottom. Its daily RSI is flirting with oversold territory that may trigger a relief bounce, but that’s not enough to confirm a trend reversal. In a bearish scenario, continued selling pressure could push ADA below its recent $0.134 support area, exposing lower price levels.

According to recent reports, crypto markets head into a holiday-shortened U.S. week with inflation data that could shape how big a rate increase the Federal Reserve will consider next month.
