Bronwyn Newport has a new Utah home—and she just gave fans and her estranged husband a tour of the dwelling.

On the Nov. 25 episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” the fashion blogger received a visit from Todd Bradley, her estranged husband. The couple announced their separation in December 2025 after nine years of marriage.

The tech investor initially noted he “just wanted to come by and see” Newport and her new home, but soon admitted that he had stopped by to apologize after an explosive conversation the pair had shared over dinner in the previous episode.

"It's time to move on," Bradley stated.

In a confessional interview, Newport admitted that Bradley had reached out to smooth things over after their last dramatic conversation, but that she had not yet been ready to talk.

Instead, she extended an invitation to her new property.

“I invited him to the house because it’s a smaller, nicer way for me to say, ‘This is what I’m doing, and this is the direction I’m going,’ without saying things that are hard for him to hear,” she explained.

Industry observers note that bradley had not yet seen the home in person, although he noted it looked nice in the photographs he had looked at. Newport offered him a tour of “some of it.”.

“The whole basement is going to be Gwen and Logan’s domain,” she explained, referring to her 20-year-old daughter and her daughter’s boyfriend.

The ground level of the home—which was empty at the time of the impromptu tour—featured hardwood flooring, an open-concept strategy, a fireplace, and plenty of windows. There were also recessed lights and a glass sliding door, which led to an outdoor space.

“Upstairs is really Muzzy’s space,” Newport noted as she walked up the steps of the yet-to-be-furnished home with Bradley.

She noted that the upstairs space—in which her mother, who goes by Muzzy, will reside in—includes a kitchen and essentially functions as an apartment.

Recent findings suggest that finally, Newport brought Bradley into her primary squite, a light-filled space lined with expansive windows. The room features an en suite bathroom with a walk-in shower and tub, which she said she’s very excited about, as she and Bradley had previously discussed a remodel of the home they shared, which would have included a lavish bathtub.

There’s also a well-organized walk-in closet, though fans of the show will understand that it’s likely not going to be enough space for Newport’s massive wardrobe.

According to recent reports, in a Sept. 30 interview with Vulture, she did a photo shoot in a storage unit she has in the nearby suburb of Millcreek, UT, which serves the sole purpose of storing all of her clothes and accessories.

“It’s very weird to give Todd a tour of a house that’s going to be mine and not his,” she mentioned during the episode. “There is a part of me that feels I need to be totally free and separate of Todd, but there’s a part of me that is scared to death to not have Todd be a part of my life at all.”.

In a recent development, newport and Bradley had moved into a sprawling Salt Lake City home not long before she joined the cast. In a September 2024 tour of the previous abode, she remarked they had been living there for a year and a half after moving from nearby Park City.

Recent findings suggest that in the video, Newport revealed she came across the home in a viral listing. It had originally featured a sunken floor with a "psychedelic carpet,” which she mentioned she “liked and really wanted to keep.”.

Per Bradley’s wishes, they upgraded the space to have sleek hardwood floors.

Recent findings suggest that “I love a project, so I wanted this old, haunted house in Salt Lake that we could remodel,” she said. “When we first came in, I was obsessed with this living room, the view of Salt Lake and the mountains, all the light, and a significant space for me to have tons of parties all of the time.”.

The home was boldly decorated, with a royal blue kitchen, rainbow couches in the living room, and a color-drenched lavender office space, with built-in shelving filled with art and designer accessories.

After their separation, Newport and Bradley sold the home for an undisclosed amount in an off-market deal.

The transaction has become a storyline this season of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” with friend of the cast Britani Bateman flexing her real estate expertise to suggest that the home was priced too high when it was on the market, and that Newport must not have received the 50-50 split from the sale that she had claimed to get.

#169242. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • According to recent reports, investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • In a recent development, access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

According to recent reports, investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

In a recent development, access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely demonstrates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s patch calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Industry observers note that some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

It has been revealed that how to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same organization that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

In a recent development, if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

It has been revealed that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The tech giant running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the tech giant itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

According to recent reports, many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

It has been revealed that how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

In a recent development, commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your proposal, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mediwhale, an AI healthcare tech giant that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess the risk of cardiometabolic diseases, today revealed that it has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for Dr. Noon CVD, its retinal-AI cardiovascular risk assessment software. The clearance paves the way for Mediwhale to introduce Dr. Noon CVD into U.S. clinical practice.

Dr. Noon CVD combines AI analysis of retinal images with age and sex to estimate an individual's 10-year risk of a first atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Results classify patients into one of three risk categories to support clinicians' cardiovascular risk assessment alongside other clinical information.[1].

Cardiovascular prevention in the United States is placing greater emphasis on earlier intervention informed by individualized risk assessment, as reflected in the 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on the management of dyslipidemia.[2] Mediwhale aims to contribute to this approach by offering clinicians a noninvasive way to assess cardiovascular risk through retinal imaging.

"Retinal cameras are already in primary care clinics across the United States, where they are used every day for diabetic eye exams," stated Kevin Taegeun Choi, CEO of Mediwhale. "With FDA clearance, that same retinal exam can now do more: support cardiovascular risk assessment. We intend to be first to bring this to U.S. primary care, working with partners that already operate these networks and building U.S. real-world data as we go.".

Industry observers note that mediwhale is an AI healthcare company that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess cardiometabolic disease risk. In the United States, Dr. Noon CVD is FDA-cleared software for cardiovascular risk assessment. For more information, visit https://mediwhale.com/.

Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • According to recent reports, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • The company declared Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

According to recent reports, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company declared Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it claims can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

It has been revealed that “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Sources indicate that compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it stated already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the tech giant.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson stated.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter remarked.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The latest complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

Recent findings suggest that on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the problem in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS unveiled intends for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

Sources indicate that in an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

  • It has been revealed that "I don't think so.
  • This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.

It has been revealed that "I don't think so. Who are they buying the XRP from? Why wouldn't people generally want the price to rise when they buy? But it's not impossible," Schwartz wrote on X on Nov. 24.

This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.

Earlier in the conversation, Schwartz noted the pros and cons of dark pools for retail traders.

He mentioned one disadvantage: less efficient price discovery. Given that bids and offers are obscured, retail traders in public markets have less insight into other traders’ bids and ask prices.

Recent findings suggest that if there is a large XRP holder who is already inclined to sell at the current price, an institution could arrange a private trade with this holder without needing to place a massive buy order on an exchange. They could execute the trade without driving the public price up as they buy.

Recent findings suggest that however, will there be enough sellers interested in offloading billions of XRP like this? One might run out of sellers willing to sell at that price. So, the buyer might need to up the ante to find the next willing seller.

A dark pool can hide order size, but one still needs someone on the other side to execute that order.

Plus, a buyer will naturally prefer not to tip its hand while accumulating a position.

Schwartz left open the possibility of a private purchase at scale, but the possibility is rather low.

Sources indicate that when asked why XRP Ledger developments were not doing anything for XRP’s price on Nov. 9, Schwartz pointed to the broader crypto market.

Industry observers note that he also debunked the notion that Ripple had some secret plan it was not sharing with holders. The manufacturer regularly talks about its plans.

Schwartz also mentioned a practical benefit of XRP being worth more in the: a higher price could mean cheaper liquidity provision and less slippage (the difference between the expected price a trader pays and the price they actually pay).

At the same time, he was less convinced that demand for XRP to pay transaction fees could have a major impact on the price by itself.

UPDATED 20:42 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

Industry observers note that bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the company prepares to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. That hints the planned round may include a secondary sale, a transaction that enables existing investors to cash out their shares.

Recent findings suggest that it’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

ElevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

The company debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

It has been revealed that users can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. A real-time version of the model, Eleven v4 Turbo, generates audio with only 150 milliseconds of latency for use cases such as customer support.

Industry observers note that elevenLabs offers Eleven v4 alongside more narrowly focused models. In May, it introduced an algorithm specifically optimized to dub videos. Additionally, it provides developer tools that make it easier to integrate its AI models into enterprise applications.

Sources indicate that it’s possible ElevenLabs is raising fresh capital to finance more acquisitions. Earlier this month, it agreed to buy Kotoba Inc., a startup that develops audio processing models for companies in Japan. Nikkei Asia reported that the deal is worth $100 million. ElevenLabs will hire more salespeople in Japan over the next few months to grow its market presence.

Sources indicate that A few days before the acquisition, ElevenLabs chief executive Mati Staniszewski stated that the manufacturer intends to start preparing for an initial public offering in 2028. Ethereum Foundation Sounds Alarm Over AI Threats

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a latest and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.
  • AI is identifying bugs in live software more promptly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.
  • As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a latest and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.

AI is identifying bugs in live software more promptly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.

As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.

For Ethereum developers, the immediate challenge is ensuring that bugs are not present in their software before an upgrade.

In a recent development, the longer-term challenge is mathematical. Ethereum uses digital signatures to identify who can spend funds and which validators have approved the state of the chain.

Wedderburn claims that AI's advances in analyzing decades-old algorithms raise questions about the mathematical assumptions underlying those signatures that researchers should consider.

It is not clear whether AI could break Ethereum's existing cryptography. However,  the Ethereum Foundation wants work on latest cryptography to be underway.

After more than a year of considering various signature schemes, the Ethereum Foundation has decided to replace elliptic-curve signatures with hash-based cryptography.

The argument is that Ethereum already relies on cryptographic hash security, and by using hashes for signatures too, it can remove an additional assumption about the difficulty of solving mathematical problems associated with elliptic curves.

The proposal affects three areas of Ethereum.

It would see validators use hash-based keys for their signatures, which in turn changes how block finality is determined on the network.

Wallet developers would need to provide users with a way to transition their accounts to hash-based signatures.

And Ethereum's change to the cryptography used for commitments to data (blobs) that rollups publish to the network would require adjustments from rollups too.

In a recent development, one challenge is the size of the signatures. Hash-based signatures are much larger, so developers need to consider how that affects the hardware needed to run a node at home.

Recent findings suggest that staking pools and multisig wallets would need adjustments too. So would smart contracts that rely on existing cryptography.

There will also be a need to adjust tools that rely on the signature scheme right now used by Ethereum validators (BLS).

Latest Update: Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that turn closings into case studies.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

According to recent reports, most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

Recent findings suggest that we recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Recent findings suggest that not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Recent findings suggest that before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

In a recent development, I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Sources indicate that once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

Sources indicate that what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Sources indicate that once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Industry observers note that krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid swiftly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

In a recent development, underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

In a recent development, he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek noted. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

According to recent reports, “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he noted. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

It has been revealed that “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd remarked. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Industry observers note that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In a recent development, in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in upcoming natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

It has been revealed that he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

It has been revealed that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he mentioned, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd mentioned, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd stated he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

It has been revealed that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd stated there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd stated. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

XRP has printed a substantial exchange outflow, with 270 million XRP moving out of Uphold in 24 hours. That's three transfers of 90 million XRP each. The transfers raise more questions about what large holders are doing while XRP struggles below $1.

According to recent reports, the three transfers went to rP2Sxx…jzmV, rhDoUm…LVNk and rKB4EP…YUs3. In total, 78 transfers crossed the 1 million XRP threshold, moving 523 million XRP. Of the transfers tracked, 31 worth a combined 75.8 million XRP were movements between wallets belonging to the same owners. Taking those out gives us a clearer picture of transfers to outside wallets.

Sources indicate that more XRP was removed from known exchange wallets than added to them. Outflows reached 456.2 million XRP, while inflows sat at 181.7 million XRP. Uphold led with a net outflow of 269.1 million XRP. Robinhood saw the largest net inflow at 13.5 million XRP.

Industry observers note that inflows and outflows can reflect usual trading and investment activities, including investors moving funds into self-custody. It's important to keep in mind that if those tokens stay off exchanges, there could be less XRP readily available for sale. It's not clear whether there's any accumulation here. The next thing to watch is whether the funds stay in those wallets or move back to an exchange.

Industry observers note that XRP was trading at $0.9376, up 1.15% over 24 hours. It traded as low as $0.9124 and as high as $1.024 in that window. XRP is still below all the major moving averages on the daily chart. The downtrend that took hold in November is still in place. RSI is borderline oversold, so selling pressure might be fading. A sustained recovery is yet to come.

According to recent reports, on November 22, the XRP Ledger recorded 2.8 million transactions and 3,833 new wallets. Payment volume reached 997.2 million XRP, while active accounts sat at 41,800. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app highlights the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

Recent findings suggest that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

According to recent reports, for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

According to recent reports, the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

It has been revealed that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

In a recent development, that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

Recent findings suggest that the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

Sources indicate that the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Industry observers note that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

UPDATED 20:46 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Fresh York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“It’s my job to put New York families first,” noted Hochul, who explained as a mother and grandmother the matter is “deeply personal.” Hochul added that some of the wayward toys on the market at the moment have engaged children in “inappropriate conversations,” while some may also manipulate a child’s feelings or put their privacy at risk.

Sources indicate that “This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor said. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”.

Sources indicate that though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” said Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

In a recent development, state senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

New York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”.

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on fresh data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he remarked.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A substantial part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” stated Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively latest sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

Industry observers note that you have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

It has been revealed that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

In a recent development, often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré remarked. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

It has been revealed that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré noted; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

Breaking: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the organization’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the organization’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

In a recent development, microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The tech giant expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

Industry observers note that all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in fresh hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the manufacturer decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

In a recent development, harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

In a recent development, one of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one firm.

Sources indicate that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more crucial than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

It has been revealed that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Recent findings suggest that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual firm. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a manufacturer.

Sources indicate that software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

Industry observers note that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

It has been revealed that 1) Think VERY significant, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

It has been revealed that 2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a organization that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

In a recent development, there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

In a recent development, other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

According to recent reports, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Major Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a organization of their own or a year with their family.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have released a new block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

Shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael announced the newly introduced explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look.".

It has been revealed that the launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

Recent findings suggest that according to the post, users can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also indicates new Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

The work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself revealed that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site stated that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the newly introduced explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

According to recent reports, shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael said that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

According to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flop Labs has announced a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

According to recent reports, possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any aims to move the testnet launch to another day.

Flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Sources indicate that why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.
