📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Industry observers note that A newly introduced baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Recent findings suggest that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

Sources indicate that to spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has complications with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and Latest Jersey.

Recent findings suggest that gangiredla mentioned the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla stated. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

According to recent reports, birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

It has been revealed that the impossible research burden on latest parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

Sources indicate that how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your organization?

In a recent development, it’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

In a recent development, that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Recent findings suggest that turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our company has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

XRP has completed a short-term golden cross against Bitcoin, giving bulls a fresh technical signal as the cryptocurrency eyes a retest of $1.

The 50 MA rose above the 200 MA on the 3-hour chart, completing a golden cross, as XRP saw relative outperformance against Bitcoin. The timing of the golden cross remains surprising given the current selling in the market.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 5.83% in the last 24 hours to $0.923, giving back most of a rally that sharply took it past $1 after Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia.

On Monday, Nvidia shocked the markets with the surprise announcement of Jensen Huang returning as the CEO of the popular tech and AI company. For crypto traders, the initial response looked extremely encouraging as most tokens sharply rose. However, the rebound began fading, with most cryptocurrencies seeing visible losses in an ongoing selloff in the early Tuesday session.

Bitcoin was down 5.23% in the last 24 hours to $60,298, with total liquidations across the crypto market reaching $596 million.

The $1 price point remains significant for XRP as it is slightly above the lower boundary of the channel in which XRP traded in recent months.

Sources indicate that XRP failed to break above the $1.55 resistance at the top of the channel and completed a full reversal toward the channel’s lower boundary at $0.99. XRP broke below this key support level in the past week, cascading to a low of $0.86, last seen in November 2024.

This drop also coincided with a death cross on the daily chart of its USD pairing, the first such occurrence in 2026. For the bearish outlook to weaken, XRP would need to reclaim $0.99 as support.

In a recent development, XRP's attempt to return above $1 has met a brick wall since mid-November. On November 18, XRP's price rise stopped exactly at $1, before it started to decline again.

On November 23, 2026, XRP tried to break above $1 again after reaching $1.02, but bulls could not hold the momentum. If the price goes above $1, XRP will target $1.21 and $1.40. On the downside, key support is expected near $0.80 and $0.64.

  • Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.
  • According to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:20 EST / NOVEMBER 26 2026.

Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or more than 9% of its workforce.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.

According to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028. That may mean the layoffs will mainly affect employees in other markets. The report indicates that SAP’s product, engineering and sales units are expected to see the largest cuts.

Executives have reportedly also asked other departments to find cost reduction opportunities.

The reported restructuring push follows a banner quarter for SAP. The firm’s sales and adjusted profit both topped analyst expectations. Its €24.11 billion cloud contract backlog, a measure of future revenue, also came in ahead of the consensus estimate.

The planned layoffs are mentioned to be connected to SAP’s efforts to integrate more artificial intelligence features into its products. The manufacturer is best known for its ERP, or enterprise resource planning, software. Enterprises use it to automate a long list of backoffice tasks and share data between teams. SAP also sells cloud services for other use cases such as sales automation and customer support.

According to recent reports, at a May user conference, the company introduced an AI interface called Joule Work for its applications. SAP says that the tool will enable workers to centrally access its products instead of navigating multiple screens.

According to recent reports, joule Work made its debut alongside a suite of AI agents dubbed Joule Assistants. According to SAP, they will use over 200 subagents to automate repetitive business tasks. Another fresh offering, Industry AI, will automate sector-specific workflows.

Industry observers note that the report that SAP is preparing for job cuts doesn’t come as a complete surprise. Last week, Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam told attendees of an investor event that the tech giant expects its headcount to decline. Additionally, two of the software maker’s six directors will reportedly leave in connection with its shift to a more AI-centric strategy.

It’s unclear when the job cuts will take place. According to Bloomberg, SAP historically revealed workforce reduction programs in January. The software maker took that route with its last major restructuring initiative, which saw it axe about 10,000 roles in 2024. The initiative cost about €3 billion.

The firm noted in a statement that “SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot demonstrates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot demonstrates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham notes those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

According to recent reports, the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own customers. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Industry observers note that binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

According to recent reports, while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now reveals:.

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what customers hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, indicated BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

According to recent reports, not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance notes it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It demonstrates the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

In a recent development, binance notes the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

Sources indicate that what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

In a recent development, binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Fresh York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He mentioned he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

Recent findings suggest that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

Sources indicate that his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Recent findings suggest that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

In a recent development, “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

In a recent development, sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

In a recent development, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it highlighted cold.

Sources indicate that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova stated. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Recent findings suggest that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Recent findings suggest that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova remarked. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

In a recent development, andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney stated.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She claims music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

In a recent development, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Sources indicate that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

Sources indicate that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

It has been revealed that she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea claims she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

In a recent development, marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Industry observers note that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

According to recent reports, “Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Recent findings suggest that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

In a recent development, kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

Recent findings suggest that so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova noted, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

#169185. Why biodiversity belongs in the master plan

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why biodiversity belongs in the master plan

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking.
  • Parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment.
  • Pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking. Decisions about infrastructure, open space, water, landscaping and mobility made early in the planning process shape how a community functions decades later.

Parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment. But there’s growing evidence that designing those landscapes to support biodiversity can help that investment do more. Planned early as part of the infrastructure conversation, biodiversity can help a community better manage water, withstand environmental stress and create stronger connections between residents and the natural environment.

Pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin. Bees, butterflies and other pollinators help many flowering plants reproduce, sustaining vegetation that supports broader ecosystems.

Development decisions can remove or fragment the food sources and nesting areas those species need. At the scale of a master-planned community, developers have an opportunity to connect habitat across parks, drainage corridors and neighborhoods, making conservation part of the places people use every day.

Developers already expect infrastructure to serve a defined purpose and perform over time. Landscape systems deserve the same scrutiny.

A stormwater basin can manage runoff while also providing habitat. A trail corridor can connect residents to destinations while connecting pollinators to food and nesting resources. Plant selection can account for seasonal habitat needs alongside appearance and maintenance.

Recent findings suggest that these decisions are much more than aesthetic considerations. A 2024 npj Urban Sustainability review examining research across stormwater management, water purification, heat mitigation, infrastructure resilience and maintenance costs found that biodiversity can meaningfully influence how blue-green infrastructure performs. More diverse ecological systems were associated with benefits ranging from improved stormwater retention and water purification to greater resilience under changing environmental conditions.

According to recent reports, for developers, the implication is practical: Ecological and engineering performance do not necessarily need to be treated as separate objectives. Incorporating habitat into drainage or open-space looks creates opportunities to serve multiple purposes within the same land area. It also brings stewardship into the budget early, when responsibilities can be assigned, and maintenance requirements can inform design.

Sources indicate that the value of parks, trails and public spaces extends beyond a direct line-item return. Planning those landscapes to support biodiversity adds another dimension to that investment, allowing them to contribute to ecological health while serving the needs of the community.

Pollinators depend on more than a patch of flowers. They need plants that provide resources throughout the growing season, places to nest and landscapes they can move through. An isolated garden may offer some of those resources, but a coordinated network can support them across a larger area.

Recent findings suggest that research indicates how much landscape design can matter. A 2026 study published in Urban Ecosystems compared two newly developed residential neighborhoods and found that pollinator abundance and diversity were two to three times higher in the neighborhood dominated by native plants than in one with conventional landscaping. Despite similar numbers of flowers, the difference suggests that what developers plant can matter as much as how much they plant.

Master-planned communities have an unusual ability to create that network. Developers overseeing hundreds or thousands of acres can coordinate planting and habitat connections across property lines and development phases.

Sources indicate that rather than treating pollinator-friendly landscaping as a one-time intervention, the strategy needs to evolve alongside the community. Establishing baseline ecological conditions before construction and continuing monitoring as development progresses creates a reference point to evaluate changes over time.

It has been revealed that that approach also requires considering habitat connectivity throughout the development process. Native plantings, open spaces and landscape corridors can be incorporated into the broader proposal, rather than treated as isolated conservation features.

As developers, we routinely track home sales, water use, construction costs and other indicators of a community’s performance. Tracking ecological outcomes brings that same discipline to landscape investments.

At Baseline, a 1,100-acre master-planned community in Broomfield, Colorado, Butterfly Pavilion introduced its Pollinator District model in 2019, integrating conservation into development and ongoing operations. With monitoring in place before construction, researchers recorded 3,805 macropollinators in developed areas in 2025, up from 587 in 2023, an increase of more than 500%.

Recent findings suggest that but numbers alone don’t tell the full story. Much of the increase came from nonnative western honeybees, making pollinator diversity an equally important measure of progress. The findings also highlight opportunities for additional native plantings to better support native bees.

The broader lesson is that ecological performance can be measured, and those findings can inform future decisions. Pollinator counts alone cannot establish the impact of every landscape intervention, but monitoring provides a way to identify changes, evaluate habitat strategies and adjust as development progresses.

Recent findings suggest that that same principle can apply beyond pollinators. Whether evaluating stormwater systems, native landscaping or habitat corridors, establishing meaningful measures of performance can help developers better understand the long-term outcomes of their investments.

According to recent reports, integrating biodiversity also creates an ongoing opportunity to learn. Working with ecological specialists helps developers understand the starting landscape, set meaningful goals and see how it responds. That work needs to carry into everyday landscape care, from what gets planted to how areas are mowed and pests are managed, with resources and responsibility for stewardship established for the years ahead.

Recent findings suggest that monitoring can guide future plant selections and help identify gaps in habitat connections as new neighborhoods take shape. It also requires consistency and an understanding that ecological conditions vary with weather, seasonal timing and other factors.

Protected lands and conservation areas remain essential to ecological health, but developed communities can contribute, too. Places designed for people can also provide meaningful habitat when ecological considerations are incorporated into planning and long-term operations.

In a recent development, for developers, this is part of the longer commitment that comes with creating a master-planned community. These are places people will call home for decades, and caring for their ecological health is another part of planning for how they perform and evolve over that same horizon.

  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal consumers that Microsoft To Do would be their newly introduced home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the tech giant’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft states Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

According to recent reports, why Microsoft is doing it: The company remarked putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A fresh Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft revealed Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Industry observers note that rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and remarked it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the tech giant in 2020.

It has been revealed that reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist owners may end up back with the people who built it.

With the Bitcoin bear market still persisting, Grayscale has sparked discussions across the crypto market after drawing attention toward a major bearish milestone for the asset.

Earlier today, Grayscale revealed that Bitcoin's current bear market has lasted more than 411 days and is becoming the longest on record.

While this marks an historic milestone in the Bitcoin bear market, Grayscale further disclosed an interesting twist that makes the current bear market pretty different from previous times.

The source confirmed that this bear market has been relatively mild in terms of price losses despite lasting longer than previous downturns.

All through the current bear market, Bitcoin has only posted a price decrease 56%, suggesting that it has suffered considerably smaller losses than several previous bear markets.

This means that even though Bitcoin has spent more than a year in a bear market, its decline has not been as severe as those seen in earlier cycles.

To back the data, Grayscale demonstrated charts comparing Bitcoin's performance across historical bear markets that ended in June 2011, December 2013, December 2017, November 2021, and the ongoing October 2025 cycle.

While the 2011, 2017 and 2021 bear cycles suffered massive losses, especially during the former when its indexed performance fell below 10, the current 2025 bear market broke historical pattern by enduring a longer period yet a comparatively modest decline in Bitcoin’s price.

Maximum discounts and other limitations may apply depending on how the rate sale is combined with other programs, the company clarified.

November’s rate sale is not Chase’s first promotion this year.

In September, the lender offered qualified borrowers up to 0.25 percentage points off mortgage rates on purchase and refinance loans. The tech giant also ran promotions in May, covering purchase and refinance loans, and in March, when it offered discounted rates on new purchase and refi loans.

Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

According to recent reports, the company declared Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it notes can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is at the moment in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this massive news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • In a recent development, the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

In a recent development, the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Recent findings suggest that testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

It has been revealed that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

Industry observers note that the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows upgrade used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

Sources indicate that so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July revision was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

It has been revealed that first, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Recent findings suggest that third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report indicates.

According to recent reports, the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

It has been revealed that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft notes it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

According to recent reports, it also looks to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

According to recent reports, microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

It has been revealed that the report also confirms what Microsoft remarked the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the organization claims, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S.
  • ‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees new ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.

According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S. derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses.

‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov. 23.

As per the guidance, these companies must maintain sufficient financial resources to cover their operating costs for at least a year.

It has been revealed that as clarified by CFTC staff, Bitcoin and Ether can be used to meet this requirement (as well as payment stablecoins). The advisory also provides guidance on how staff interpret the current rules. It also applies to swap execution facilities (SEFs), which are platforms where counterparties trade swaps.

According to recent reports, bitcoin holdings worth $10 million could count for $8 million toward the annual requirement, based on the minimum 20% discount that CFTC staff mentioned they would accept. This provides some flexibility in case Bitcoin's price falls. The discount is also called a haircut.

In a recent development, for Ether, the same minimum 20% haircut applies. For payment stablecoins, the haircut is 2%.

Recent findings suggest that this provides some incentive for an exchange to actually hold BTC. Exchanges could hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets and use some of its value to satisfy this reserve requirement. There would be no need to sell it for USD first.

It has been revealed that however, a futures exchange still needs to have sufficient unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover its operating costs for at least six months. Bitcoin, Ether and even payment stablecoins do not fall into this category.

In a recent development, the same six-month liquidity requirement applies to clearinghouses. Additionally, they need to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover a default by a clearing member.

It has been revealed that CFTC staff also noted a potential downside for exchanges holding crypto reserves. During a market slump, there's a risk that an exchange's operating losses might rise. At the same time, the value of the Bitcoin it holds to cover those losses might fall.

So this possibility should be considered before an exchange decides whether to use Bitcoin to meet its financial resource requirements.

UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 27 2026.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Jensen Huang’s back, and not everyone is happy with that.

Nvidia’s board reversed the resignation of its former and current-again CEO Monday, apparently under pressure from the well-known business genius and lame-duck President Donald Trump, who worried that the stock market and the AI trade would suffer without him at the helm.

Huang (pictured) clearly has management talent, having built one of the most valuable companies in the world. But his return, amid continuing revelations and questions about Nvidia’s business, sets an awful precedent in business. No one person should be too important to fail, and Huang set up a corporate structure that courts disaster if he’s forced to leave again or gets run over by a bus. That’s a world-class failure of a CEO and his board at one of their most basic jobs, and his tech-bro enablers should know better than to clamor for his return.

According to recent reports, after all, internal and government investigations continue, as more details come to light about probably the worst of the whole affair(s). It’s clear that at a time when there’s existential worry about China closing the U.S. lead in AI — a potential defense and cybersecurity disaster — the chief supplier of AI chips was allowing cutting-edge chips to be sent to China. (Thankfully, that loophole may be about to close.) Oh, and this week’s stock market pretty much discounted much of the supposed benefit Huang’s reinstatement was supposed to provide.

So what are we left with? The CEO of the pivotal company in AI is back with not even a slap on the wrist, let alone any consequences for multiple affairs — one with a woman who shuttled both barred GPUs and apparently inside information to China, another with an Nvidia VP, plus at least a couple others he fessed up to. Oh, and he lied about them until he couldn’t anymore. Any semblance of corporate governance and ethics — at Nvidia and everywhere else by example — is utterly torched.

It has been revealed that hey, if you think that’s a buying opportunity, I’ve got some high-end GPUs in Singapore to sell you. Anyway, let’s move on before I tell you what I really think.

According to recent reports, paul Gillin dove into why open-weight AI models that enterprises can tailor to their specific needs are taking off this year. “The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management,” he notes. “Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task.”.

Sources indicate that last week Palo Alto Networks stated it will acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. This week was CrowdStrike’s turn, as it pulled the trigger on buying Zscaler for a pretty stunning $44 billion. As AI makes cyberattacks far easier and more numerous, it seems a sure bet that today’s rickety cybersecurity industry with hundred of point products won’t stand.

AI continues to be a big driver of upside earnings surprises, but investors increasingly wary of AI spending are all over the place. Dell in particular more than doubled its revenue, only to see its shares go nowhere Wednesday, while HP got hit by the PC slowdown but saw its shares rise more than 12%. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • According to recent reports, most stablecoin rolls out promise a token that never moves.
  • Industry observers note that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

According to recent reports, most stablecoin rolls out promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

Industry observers note that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The tech giant states R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

It has been revealed that the project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery stated the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it significant" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the manufacturer, cost nothing.

Recent findings suggest that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Industry observers note that ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as upcoming rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he mentioned, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

Industry observers note that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

It has been revealed that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on organization disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

Industry observers note that for everyday owners, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Each account trading on the XRP Ledger's decentralized exchange moved an average of 4,328 XRP a day in the third quarter of 2026, up 437% from 805 XRP in the same quarter a year earlier, according to a report that XRP treasury manufacturer Evernorth released on Tuesday.

According to Evernorth, the average swap on the XRP Ledger reached 35 XRP in the third quarter, up from 19 XRP in the second quarter and under 6 XRP a year earlier. "The growth came from bigger trades, not more of them," the organization wrote in the report.

According to recent reports, at the same time, the number of accounts trading on the XRP Ledger's order book fell to 1,042 a day in the third quarter of 2026 from 2,027 a day in the third quarter of 2025. The number stood at 1,203 in the fourth quarter of 2025, 1,324 in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,125 in the second quarter, according to the report.

Order-book volume on the XRP Ledger rose to 4.51 million XRP a day in the third quarter from 1.63 million XRP a day a year earlier, Evernorth data reveals.

In total, 5.16 million XRP a day was traded on the XRP Ledger's exchange in the third quarter, and the figure was up 96% year over year, according to Evernorth.

Sources indicate that measured in U.S. dollars, exchange volume on the XRP Ledger fell 15% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the report.

Recent findings suggest that evernorth also compared the XRP Ledger with Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche and Polygon. Across these seven networks, exchange volume in dollars fell 42% over the same period, the report demonstrates.

XRP was trading at around $0.93 on Tuesday morning after reaching as high as $1.026 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap.

The report also demonstrates that the average balance of Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin on the XRP Ledger reached $937 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from $539 million in the second quarter. By the end of the quarter, the RLUSD balance on the XRP Ledger stood at $1.15 billion, compared with $670 million at the end of the second quarter, and the number of RLUSD holders on the network rose to 67,449 from 45,620.

According to recent reports, according to Evernorth, the XRP Ledger's average share of RLUSD reached 48.5% in the third quarter, up from 34% in the second quarter. Still, Ethereum finished the quarter with more RLUSD than the XRP Ledger. Evernorth noted that on Ethereum, RLUSD "can already be lent," and that on the XRP Ledger, "native lending is in validator voting.".

Sources indicate that as of Nov. 20, the Lending Protocol amendment had 24 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. The amendment needs 29 votes, held for 14 days, to activate.

Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9, and its shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN on Oct. 12. The manufacturer entered the public markets holding approximately 473 million XRP, according to its press release.

Evernorth declared the deal in October 2025, with investments from SBI, Ripple, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas J. McInerney, president and CEO of Genworth Financial, has stepped down from his roles at the organization and its board of directors to focus on his health, the company announced. The board appointed Jerome T. Upton, its current chief financial officer, as president, CEO and director. Upton will remain CFO through Dec. 31, with Angela Simmons expected to assume the role on Jan. 1, 2027.

Fannie Mae appointed David Shafer to its board of directors effective Nov. 23. His term will end at the next annual board election, or if he resigns or is removed by the Federal Housing Finance Agency. His committee assignments have not yet been determined.

It has been revealed that the organization also entered into retention agreements with four executives totaling $4.75 million. Chief financial officer Chryssa Halley and chief investment officer Erik Bisso will each receive $1.5 million, multifamily executive vice president Kelly Follain will receive $1 million, and chief risk officer Anthony Moon will receive $750,000.

The awards will be paid in two equal installments, in December 2026 and December 2027, provided the executives remain employed and comply with the agreements, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In a recent development, the Federal Home Loan Bank of Newly introduced York elected Charles E. Kilbourne, managing director of the Financial Services Volunteer Corps and an independent director since 2019, as board chair for a two-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Kilbourne, who chairs the board’s housing committee, will succeed Chris Martin, who is retiring at the end of this year after more than a decade of service.

Element Home Loans, a division of NFM Lending, has hired Darrell Boan as branch manager in Greensboro, North Carolina, as the company expands its presence in the Southeast. Boan, who has more than 25 years of mortgage industry experience, will lead local growth, support loan originators, and build relationships with clients and community partners.

The cryptocurrency market delivered a welcome dose of relief over the past 24 hours. Bitcoin reclaimed the $60,000 level, rising roughly 2.5–3.5% to trade between $60,400 and $60,800, while the broader market advanced in tandem.

Ethereum climbed to the $1,690–$1,710 range, XRP advanced toward $0.95–$0.96, and total crypto market capitalization pushed higher toward $2.15–$2.16 trillion.

After weeks of heavy selling and extreme fear, the bounce has sparked renewed discussion about whether this could mark the early stages of a more sustained recovery heading into 2027.

Prices became deeply oversold after Bitcoin’s slide toward the mid-$50,000s earlier in the week, with short-term RSI readings hitting extreme lows that historically attract dip-buyers and mean-reversion algorithms.

Recent findings suggest that forced short covering amplified the move higher as leveraged bearish positions were liquidated. A concurrent recovery in technology and AI-related equities improved broader risk appetite, and crypto’s high correlation with those sectors helped lift digital assets.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents stated.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Industry observers note that pierpoint mentioned he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

Industry observers note that white also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton remarked it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

According to recent reports, pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also remarked the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Sources indicate that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

In a recent development, pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

Sources indicate that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.
