Latest Update: Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • Industry observers note that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • In a recent development, attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

Industry observers note that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley stated that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

In a recent development, attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals concern ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Sources indicate that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Recent findings suggest that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

It has been revealed that AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella notes his firm’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he remarked at the Latest York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a manufacturer’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It has been revealed that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

Sources indicate that there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

The referral source real estate agents overlook is sitting in the next office

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve spent more than 25 years in this business, and one pattern has held strong in every market I’ve worked in: the agents who build lasting careers rarely do it alone.
  • Referrals between agents get less attention than they deserve.
  • Recent findings suggest that your brokerage is the most natural place to begin, and it’s often the most overlooked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve spent more than 25 years in this business, and one pattern has held strong in every market I’ve worked in: the agents who build lasting careers rarely do it alone. They have a network of fellow agents who think of them first when a client needs help. At The Agency, we were built on that idea. We encourage our agents to reach across the aisle, even to competitors, because when agents collaborate, more deals get done and clients are better served.

Referrals between agents get less attention than they deserve. We talk constantly about our sphere of influence, past clients and social media. Yet a colleague who’s relocating a client to your market, or who’s overbooked and can’t take on a fresh listing, might hand you a deal worth far more than a month of lead generation. Those opportunities only come to agents who’ve earned a place in someone’s mind.

Recent findings suggest that your brokerage is the most natural place to begin, and it’s often the most overlooked. Most of us share an office, a leadership team and a set of tools with dozens or even hundreds of agents, and many of us barely know their names.

Introduce yourself. Show up at the sales meeting, the training and the broker open, and stay for the conversation afterward. Ask people what they specialize in, what kind of client they love working with, and what they’d happily hand off. You’ll learn who’s the go-to for condos, who knows the hillside neighborhoods best, and who’s the strongest negotiator in the building.

That knowledge pays off quickly. When a client mentions a need outside your expertise, you’ll know exactly who to call. When a colleague gets a request that fits your strengths, they’ll know to call you. Trust inside a brokerage builds slowly, but once it’s there, it makes everyone’s business stronger.

It has been revealed that competition is part of this industry, and I won’t pretend otherwise. But the agent across the street at another firm is also a potential partner, and the best ones treat them that way.

Recent findings suggest that think about how much of real estate is geographic. Clients move across the country, across the state, sometimes across town into a different market. Your client in Los Angeles who’s buying in Aspen needs someone they can trust on the ground, and you can’t be that person. A thoughtful agent in Aspen, whom you’ve met and vetted, can. The same goes in reverse. That’s a referral built on mutual respect, and it often leads to repeat business flowing both ways for years.

Industry events, local board committees and MLS involvement are all excellent places to meet these people. You see how people handle disagreement, how they treat staff, and how they follow through. That’s the kind of insight no online profile will give you.

If you want referrals, you have to be worth referring. When one agent sends a client to another, they’re putting their own reputation on the line. They want to know that their client will be taken care of, that communication will be prompt, and that the deal will be handled with integrity.

So treat every interaction with another agent as an audition, whether or not it’s a referral situation. Return calls swiftly. Show up prepared. Be the person who makes a tough negotiation easier instead of harder. Agents remember who was gracious under pressure, and they remember who wasn’t.

Close the loop, too. If someone sends you a client, keep them updated and thank them, even when the deal takes months. It sounds small, but plenty of agents forget, and the ones who don’t stand out.

I’d encourage agents to build  a simple structure around this. Set a goal to connect with a few fresh agents each month, one or two inside your brokerage and a few outside it. Grab coffee or hop on a quick call. Send a note when you see a colleague’s listing go under contract. Ask how you can be useful before you ask for anything.

It doesn’t take much time, just consistency and a willingness to see other agents as allies. Your next client might be working with an agent down the hall right now, or with one in a brokerage across the country. Sooner or later, that client will ask for a recommendation. Make sure the agent who gets asked already knows you.

Rainy Hake Austin is a brokerage leader at The Agency.

According to the feature, beginner ballroom dancing is designed with newly introduced dancers in mind, allowing students to learn at a comfortable pace without feeling pressured to keep up with anyone else.

Readers learn that a first ballroom lesson typically begins with a conversation between the student and the dance instructor. This discussion helps the instructor understand each student's goals, whether they are preparing for a wedding, looking for a latest hobby, or simply interested in learning ballroom dance lessons for fun. The article notes that understanding these goals allows instruction to be tailored to each student's comfort level.

The feature also emphasizes that no prior dance experience is necessary. Many students arrive for their first ballroom lesson without knowing any dance steps, and instructors expect beginners to start from the basics. According to the article, lessons are structured to introduce simple movements one at a time, helping students develop confidence as each new skill builds naturally on the last.

These concepts provide the foundation for future ballroom dance lessons while remaining approachable for new students. Readers also learn that students can participate whether they arrive with a partner or attend alone. The article explains that many dance studios provide instructors or practice partners when needed, allowing anyone interested in beginner ballroom dancing to participate comfortably. Another point highlighted in the article is that making mistakes is an expected part of learning. The dance instructor encourages questions, provides corrections, and allows students time to practice without feeling rushed. Rather than viewing mistakes as setbacks, the article describes them as valuable opportunities that help students improve with each lesson.

Instead of introducing numerous dances at once, instructors typically focus on mastering a few basic movements correctly before moving forward. This steady approach helps students retain what they have learned while building confidence through consistent progress.

The article also offers practical guidance about preparing for the lesson itself. Comfortable clothing that allows easy movement and secure shoes are generally all that is needed for a first visit to a dance studio. Special dance attire is rarely necessary, allowing beginners to focus on learning rather than worrying about what to wear.

As the lesson concludes, many students discover they have learned more than they expected in a single session. The article notes that initial nervousness often gives way to confidence as basic movements become more familiar. Regular ballroom dance lessons continue to build on that foundation, helping students develop new skills while enjoying the movement, social connection, and satisfaction that come with steady improvement.

Industry observers note that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

It has been revealed that the most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also mentioned it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

It has been revealed that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

In a recent development, the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

In a recent development, that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

It has been revealed that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

It has been revealed that this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Sources indicate that legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

According to recent reports, A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself states the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the problems presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

Industry observers note that in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a organization, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

It has been revealed that the practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

Industry observers note that the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

UPDATED 16:32 EST / NOVEMBER 27 2026.

Recent findings suggest that hackers have reportedly breached Cloud One, a platform that the U.S. Air Force uses to power dozens of internal applications.

Reuters broke the news today, citing three people familiar with the matter. The news agency reported that the cyberattack could “jeopardize a vast swath” of sensitive data.

Cloud One runs on infrastructure from Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Oracle Corp. and Google LLC. The applications that it powers perform a wide range of tasks. Some are designed to ease administrative chores such as managing personnel records, while others analyze radar data and track the location of hardware assets.

It has been revealed that the breach was reportedly discovered “within the past month or so.” Technical personnel spotted malicious activity while performing a system upgrade. According to Reuters, the investigators probing the incident have asked the U.S. Cyber Command to assist with the analysis.

Many key details about the cyberattack, including when it started, remain unclear. However, today’s report did specify that the breach saw hackers gain access to Cloud One’s control plane.

According to recent reports, A control plane is a software engine that coordinates a technology system’s other components. Its role varies based on the system that it powers. The Kubernetes control plane, for example, performs tasks such as spinning up containers, while a network’s control plane coordinates the flow of traffic.

In a recent development, reuters’ sources said that the Cloud One control plane can theoretically be used to check the operational status of Air Force assets. However, it’s unclear whether hackers stole any sensitive data.

The attackers reportedly compromised Cloud One via a software vulnerability. The report didn’t specify whether the flaw was in a custom software component or an external, off-the-shelf product. In the latter scenario, other organizations that use the off-the-shelf product may also be vulnerable.

Hackers often chain together multiple vulnerabilities rather than relying on a single flaw. Additionally, they’re increasingly using artificial intelligence to speed up cyberattacks.

Earlier this week, the Latest York Times reported that a threat actor had breached a data analysis system used by the U.S. intelligence community. The hackers used an open-source AI cyberattack tool called ARTEX. The breach reportedly didn’t compromise any classified data.

In a recent development, according to Reuters, the Air Force has paused an internal project focused on moving legacy applications to Cloud One. It also blocked updates to workloads that already run on the platform. That left personnel unable to patch applications against a “new batch of serious software vulnerabilities.” The report suggests that the vulnerabilities were in off-the-shelf software that is also used by other organizations.

The Cloud One hack and the recent ARTEX-powered breach continue a string of recent cyberattacks against the federal government. Earlier this week, the U.S. Treasury Department reportedly took parts of its infrastructure offline in response to a cyber incident. A few days earlier, sources told NBC News reported that hackers had breached a payment system used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

#169161. Who should referee a national MLS, brokers or a neutral body?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1162 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Who should referee a national MLS, brokers or a neutral body?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when Open Real Estate was confirmed, the question of a national listing system moved back to the center of our industry.
  • According to recent reports, first, credit where it is due.
  • I see two problems, one practical and one structural, and the structural one is the one that should concern every leader who does not run one of the three or four largest firms in the country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Open Real Estate was confirmed, the question of a national listing system moved back to the center of our industry. I am early in my read on this particular initiative. But I have spent a long time on the underlying question, enough that I have written a white paper of more than 70 pages on why a broker-controlled national MLS is the wrong design and what a right one would look like. For the leaders reading this, I want to lay out the core of that thinking, because this is a decision our industry may actually make in the next few years, and we should make it with our eyes open.

According to recent reports, first, credit where it is due. A coalition of large brokerages banded together and put their names to a public position. That takes coordination and conviction, and it is plainly a response to a real and growing trend, the migration of listings into private and exclusive channels that never touch the open market. The concern is legitimate. When inventory moves into walled gardens, buyers see less, agents compete on access instead of expertise, and the consumer is quietly disadvantaged. Leaders who are worried about that are worried about the right thing.

I see two problems, one practical and one structural, and the structural one is the one that should concern every leader who does not run one of the three or four largest firms in the country.

The practical problem is straightforward. The founders have mentioned that Open Real Estate is not a national MLS and is not meant to replace local MLSs. Whatever we call it, it is built to function as shared national listing infrastructure, and that infrastructure includes a participant view option, where a listing can be seen only by agents at participating brokerages and cannot be publicly marketed by anyone. In other words, the model does not stop private listings. It gives them a larger, better-organized home. The exact behavior this is meant to counter can continue, and we have built a bigger shared system that still has walls inside it.

Consider the architecture we have now. Hundreds of local MLSs operate across the country. We complain about that fragmentation endlessly, and it does create real friction for agents and consumers. But the fragmentation also delivers a benefit almost no one names. Each MLS acts as its own silo, its own firewall. Because the data lives in hundreds of independent repositories, no single company controls the national market. There is a series called Silo that captures the idea well. Each silo runs itself, and no one can command the whole system. Our MLS structure has handed us that same protection almost by accident. The walls are inconvenient, and the walls are also the reason no one firm owns the country’s data.

Recent findings suggest that now collapse all of it into one national system, whatever label it carries, and ask the only question that matters. Who runs it? If the answer is that brokers run it, then the brokers with the deepest pockets will control the nation’s listing infrastructure. The independents, the single-office shops, the regional firms, they will have little to no voice. Whoever sits atop a broker-controlled national system writes the rules for everyone downstream, including their direct competitors. That is not a free market with shared plumbing. That is a tollgate owned by a few, and everyone else pays to pass through.

Powerfact: Whoever controls a national MLS controls the terms of competition for every agent in the country. That cannot be a competitor.

Sources indicate that so, let me be clear that I am not against unification. A national MLS done correctly would be a real asset. It would let an agent see listings nationwide rather than stitching together access market by market. It would mean one playbook, the same rules, forms, and fields in every state, so practicing across state lines or relocating would not require relearning the mechanics each time. That consistency would benefitagents, brokers, and consumers. The debate should not be unify or do not unify. The fight is already here, and it should be about who holds the technology in the middle.

And we already have a proven answer inside our own economy. Visa and MasterCard.

Recent findings suggest that the first bank card came from Bank of America. When other banks saw it working, each began building its own card and its own processing, and the result was chaos, because every bank set different rules and the consumer experience depended on which card you carried. The resolution was not to let the largest bank operate everyone else’s cards. It was Visa, a separate entity sitting in the middle. Each bank still runs its own business and competes on its own terms. The technology and the standards that make the system uniform for the consumer are handled by a neutral party that no single bank owns.

That is the template for a national MLS. Not control by the largest brokerages, but a neutral, broker-independent organization that operates the technology and maintains uniform rules, while every brokerage, large and small, continues to run its own business and compete on skill and service. Keep each firm a silo where it should be a silo. Make the shared rails in the middle belong to no one in particular. That is the only structure that stays fair to the smallest independent and the largest franchise at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that when the next national platform is confirmed, and there will be more of them, do not evaluate it on the feature list. Evaluate it on governance. Ask who owns it, who sits on the board, how the rules get changed, and what recourse a small brokerage has if the controlling firms decide to change the terms. If the governance concentrates power in a handful of competitors, the convenience on the surface is not worth the dependency underneath. If the governance looks like Visa, neutral, independent, and accountable to all participants rather than to the biggest ones, then we may finally have something worth building.

I appreciate the effort behind Open Real Estate, and I share the concern that prompted it. But good intentions do not fix bad architecture. A national listing system run by brokers would trade the problem of private listings for the larger problem of a privatized commons, owned by the few and rented to the many. We can do better, and we have a model sitting in our wallets that demonstrates us how. Build the referee first. Then build the league.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

  • 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Do you need a trust or is a will enough?
  • The article explains that many people begin estate planning by asking whether they need a trust or a will.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jennifer McKenna explains how trusts and wills work together to support an estate planning strategy based on individual needs.

LEE'S SUMMIT, Mo., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Do you need a trust or is a will enough? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Estate Planning Attorney Jennifer McKenna of the Jennifer Ward McKenna, Attorney at Law in Lees Summit, Missouri, explains how trusts and wills serve different purposes within an estate planning strategy.

The article explains that many people begin estate planning by asking whether they need a trust or a will. The answer depends on factors such as family circumstances, financial goals, the types of assets they own, and how they want those assets managed after death. The article notes that both legal tools play important roles and understanding their differences helps individuals make informed decisions.

According to the article, a will is a legal document that explains how a person's property should be distributed after death. It also allows someone to name an executor to manage the estate and nominate guardians for minor children when necessary. The article describes a will as the foundation of many estate planning plans because it provides clear instructions and guidance for loved ones during a difficult time.

According to recent reports, the HelloNation article also explains that a will always goes through the probate process after death. During probate, the court validates the will, oversees the payment of debts, and authorizes the distribution of assets. While probate is a routine legal process, the article notes that the timeline depends on the amount of assets administered through the will, the complexity of the estate, and state law. Some estates move through probate relatively quickly, while most require several months to resolve legal or administrative matters.

A trust serves a different purpose by allowing assets to be managed by a trustee for the benefit of designated beneficiaries. Unlike a will, many assets held in a properly funded trust can pass directly to beneficiaries without going through probate. The article explains that avoiding probate is one of the primary reasons some individuals include a trust as part of an overall estate planning strategy. It also notes that a trust can provide instructions for managing assets if the person creating the trust becomes unable to manage financial matters during their lifetime or when a beneficiary is unable to manage an inheritance effectively, such as a young child or an individual with special needs.

In a recent development, the article emphasizes that a trust is not automatically the right choice for every family. Establishing and maintaining a trust requires additional planning, and assets must be properly transferred into the trust for it to function as intended. If assets remain outside the trust, they may still be subject to probate. The article explains that understanding how a trust works is just as crucial as deciding whether to create one.

Recent findings suggest that rather than viewing these documents as alternatives, the article explains that a will and a trust often work together. A trust may be used to manage significant assets, while a will can address property that was not transferred into the trust and nominate guardians for minor children. According to the article, this combination creates a more complete estate planning approach that reflects a family's specific circumstances and long-term goals.

It has been revealed that the article also notes that every estate is different, and no single solution works for everyone. Some individuals focus on protecting young children, while others are more concerned with managing business interests, real estate, or investment accounts. Estate planning allows legal documents to reflect those priorities instead of relying on general assumptions.

It has been revealed that the article concludes that delaying estate planning because of uncertainty about choosing a trust or a will can leave important questions unanswered. Learning how a trust, a will, and probate work allows individuals to make informed decisions that fit their own circumstances. Whether someone ultimately chooses a will, a trust, or both, taking time to understand these legal tools can provide greater clarity and help protect loved ones in the future.

Fidelity Investments now supports three latest cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

According to recent reports, the firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where consumers can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

In a recent development, on July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the organization introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it debuted Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible owners can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • According to recent reports, the outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

According to recent reports, the outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

It has been revealed that the new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the manufacturer-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

According to recent reports, “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Industry observers note that marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis mentioned the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Sources indicate that lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight tech giant acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a upcoming startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis remarked.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making newly introduced data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The firm isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Industry observers note that its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The tech giant indicates it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan noted that at the major tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he noted.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe notes gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Recent findings suggest that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Sources indicate that much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

It has been revealed that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe intends to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis remarked. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

In a recent development, the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis stated. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking tech giant DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

It has been revealed that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

It has been revealed that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

According to recent reports, marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis stated the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one significant customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

It has been revealed that updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Breaking: Will the Anthropic IPO supercharge San Francisco’s already-hot housing market?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on Nov.
  • The question people keep asking me is: what happens to the real estate market in San Francisco?
  • Recent findings suggest that san Francisco’s housing market was already the hottest market in the country before Anthropic’s IPO came to town.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on Nasdaq at a valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion, creating perhaps 5000 millionaires, many of whom reside in the city of San Francisco, where the company is based.

The question people keep asking me is: what happens to the real estate market in San Francisco?

Recent findings suggest that san Francisco’s housing market was already the hottest market in the country before Anthropic’s IPO came to town. While the rest of the country wrestled with mortgage rates near multi-decade highs, San Francisco faced bidding wars and intense competition. The median single-family home sale price rose 29% year over year to $2.39 million in October, the largest gain since February 2018. Some 86% of homes sold above asking price, up from 77% a year earlier.

Among 552 U.S. counties with at least 300 single-family home sales from August through October, San Francisco was the only one where prices rose more than 10%. The typical county saw prices rise just 1.9%, 149 counties recorded declines, and San Francisco homes were more than four times as likely as the typical U.S. home to sell above asking.

In past decades, a single or even a series of IPOs have not notably been a driver of the San Francisco housing market. Macro market cycles have mattered more. Notably, San Francisco home prices tend to follow the peaks and valleys of the entire Nasdaq Composite by about 9-12 months. This makes sense since any one IPO might impact the wealth of a few hundred people, where the Nasdaq represents an entire universe of tech related wealth and economic dynamism.

Compass market analyst Janel Evans-Anderson looked at 19 major tech IPOs over the last 20+ years and notes that IPOs from companies like Google, Facebook and Uber might spur some home sales, but much more crucial are the significant trends in tech and the economy.

But the scale of the Anthropic IPO, combined with San Francisco’s current housing market conditions, creates a different set of circumstances from previous technology IPOs.

The economic effects of Anthropic’s IPO may have already hit San Francisco real estate, even before employees can access the full value of their shares.

In the past, the IPO was a starting point for growth and wealth creation. Now the IPO may be the exit. For example, NVIDIA went public in 1999, but the massive wealth created by the tech giant happened nearly 20 years later. Anthropic’s IPO valuation is 100x or 1000x the old thresholds.

Employees of Anthropic and other highly-valued tech firms have access to capital in ways that were not available to tech workers 10 or 20 years ago. In the last decade, a robust secondary market for private company stock has developed. Many executives at hot AI companies (not just Anthropic) have been able to sell their shares into the secondary market for years prior to the IPO.

Equity-rich tech workers can also borrow against their shares. This financial instrument lets people access the cash, pay cash for a house, and not have to pay taxes on the sale of the stock. In decades past, when a substantial IPO was $1 billion, perhaps one or two execs at the startup would have access to this kind of borrowing. When the IPO is $1 trillion, suddenly hundreds or thousands of employees have access to capital prior to the IPO.

Sources indicate that anthropic’s IPO is introducing an enormous pool of newly liquid wealth into a housing market where prices are already rising rapidly and available homes are scarce. And because Anthropic employees face lockup restrictions, with sales limited initially to 10% of holdings and more shares unlocking through 2027, that wealth could keep reaching the housing market well into 2027.

San Francisco County was already the hottest housing market in the nation before the IPO. Among 552 U.S. counties with at least 300 single-family home sales from August through October, it was the only one where prices rose more than 10%. The typical county saw prices rise just 1.9%, while 149 counties recorded declines. Homes in San Francisco County were over four times more likely to sell for above their asking price than the typical U.S. home.

It’s not just that the IPOs are bigger now. This cash tsunami floods into a housing market that is much smaller than it used to be. There are fewer than 700 single family homes and condos for sale in the city as of the end of November 2026. That’s about 20% fewer than normal for the 2010s and is 40% fewer than in 2012 when Facebook IPO’d.

It has been revealed that when fresh purchasing power enters a market with limited inventory, competition intensifies and pushes prices higher. The imbalance is particularly striking in 2026: we’ve counted over 250 sales in the city this year that closed at least $1 million over asking.

The days since the IPO have been dramatically volatile for Anthropic shares and for the entire market. Valuations of many public tech companies have been hit by market turmoil in recent weeks. It could be that by next spring the AI bubble has popped and much of this wealth has evaporated.

Recent findings suggest that looking back on the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, that led to a sharp change in the housing market in the city. Annual home price appreciation plummeted from nearly 30% per year at the peak of the bubble to 0%. At the time, a handful of executives that had borrowed against their shares had to sell the home to pay back the loan. If the Anthropic IPO is 1000x bigger than previous events, what does a bubble burst look like this time?

Breaking: ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

According to recent reports, that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no newly introduced mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain notes nothing moves unless it passes.

According to recent reports, if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's upcoming private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a upcoming whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

Recent findings suggest that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Recent findings suggest that two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

In a recent development, on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

It has been revealed that that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the initiative, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange customers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

According to recent reports, on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain states it will announce any change to the process in advance.

According to recent reports, the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

In a recent development, taken together, this looks more like a retirement blueprint for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An investigation has linked Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia Corp.
  • In a recent development, bloomberg researched the firms in question by reviewing regulatory documents from China.
  • It has been revealed that in October, the New York Times revealed that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:13 EST / NOVEMBER 27 2026.

An investigation has linked Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia Corp. controversy, to Chinese firms that reportedly possess smuggled chips.

In a recent development, bloomberg researched the firms in question by reviewing regulatory documents from China. The paper published the results of its analysis today.

It has been revealed that in October, the New York Times revealed that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. Some U.S. officials reportedly believe she is a spy, while others see her ties to China’s intelligence service as “more circumstantial.” Nvidia’s board ousted Jensen Huang over the affair and reinstated him about two weeks later.

In a recent development, bloomberg’s investigation focused on the Yangtze River Delta Project, a data center campus in China. The paper found links between the project and Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that Alice Huang headed until last year. According to the report, Megaspeed at one point described the campus as its largest data center.

It has been revealed that the investigation also determined that the Yangtze River Delta Project’s president is a businessman called Kang Wei. Earlier reports identified him as Alice Huang’s husband.

In a recent development, bloomberg looked into a Chinese company called Shanghai Kezhan that has ties to the Yangtze River Delta Project. The company is reportedly a unit of a Japanese firm that is controlled by Alice Huang. Kezhan stated in a filing that it uses the data center to host 32 servers equipped with Nvidia’s H200 chips, which can’t be legally exported to China.

Recent findings suggest that the company also uses the facility to host a GB200 rack. GB200 systems include 72 of Nvidia’s Blackwell B200 graphics cards, which are significantly more capable than the H200. They too are subject to U.S. export restrictions.

A second Chinese organization, Shanghai Shuoyao, has reportedly deployed a GB300 rack at the data center. Such systems are based on the Blackwell Ultra, an upgraded version of the B200 that features significantly more memory. It’s Nvidia’s second fastest graphics card behind its latest Rubin accelerator.

Both Kezhan and Shuoyao described the servers in loan documents. They used the systems as collateral for millions of dollars in debt financing. According to Bloomberg, it’s possible the companies possess additional Nvidia systems but didn’t mention them in the documents because they weren’t used as collateral.

The report raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of Nvidia’s regulatory compliance efforts days before Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress. According to CNBC, he will testify before three House committees on Sunday and the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monday brought a sharp rebound across crypto markets after Bitcoin's weekend crash toward $55,000.

XRP briefly reclaimed $1 as a short squeeze followed a major Nvidia-related rally, while Strategy continued adding Bitcoin to its treasury despite the market downturn.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, U.S. authorities took action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency linked to the October Binance hack.

In a recent development, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture action on Nov. 23 seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in USDC allegedly stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers.

Recent findings suggest that the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government. The latest filing represents another step toward recovering funds following the Oct. 29 attack, which reportedly resulted in more than $6 billion in stolen cryptocurrency.

It has been revealed that the DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

Sources indicate that U.S. authorities stated they had helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in cryptocurrency since the theft. The case highlights the role of cooperation between law enforcement agencies and crypto companies in tracking and recovering stolen digital assets.

Strategy purchased another 457 BTC for approximately $29.6 million, according to a Nov. 23 report based on the firm's SEC filing.

The latest acquisition was made at an average price of $64,898 per Bitcoin, bringing Strategy's holdings to approximately 851,305 BTC. The firm has spent around $64.23 billion accumulating Bitcoin at an average purchase price of $75,446.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

XRP briefly climbed above $1 on Monday after Nvidia's Jensen Huang returned to his roles as CEO and president, triggering a sharp rally in U.S. technology stocks and broader risk assets.

On Binance's XRP/USDT perpetual contract, the token moved from approximately $0.94 to $1.02 within minutes after 14:00 UTC, before retreating to around $0.984.

CoinGlass data cited by U.Today revealed that XRP short liquidations exceeded long liquidations by 578%.

Across the crypto market, 110,663 traders were liquidated for $660.89 million over the past 24 hours, while shorts accounted for $515.94 million of that amount.

The move highlighted how quickly market sentiment can shift during a volatile rebound, particularly when leveraged traders are positioned against a sudden price increase.

Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from Newly introduced Jersey’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.
  • Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S.
  • Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith remarked the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith remarked the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he remarked most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed organization that wants to build in Finland. Google unveiled a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, mentioned he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the firm for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

It has been revealed that white House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Industry observers note that smith noted Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the firm “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered notable.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He mentioned the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he stated much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.
